lead: Every sensor in this unit ends at an electronic control unit (ECU), and every actuator starts at one. Inside the ECU sit semiconductor components (diodes, transistors, integrated circuits) and a microcontroller, a one-chip computer that reads the sensors, runs the control program and switches the outputs thousands of times a second. A car is a hard place for electronics, so these parts are built for heat, vibration and a noisy supply.
prereq: You need: Ohm's law, power P = V I = I²R, and the vehicle electrical system (12 V battery and alternator) from the batteries and charging topic.

sections.h3: Demands on automotive electronics and semiconductor basics

blocks.text: A vehicle ECU must work for 15 years or more in conditions an office computer never meets. Some syllabi list these as the demands on automotive electronics:

items: Temperature: −40 °C to +85 °C in the cabin and up to 125 °C or 150 °C on or near the engine. Automotive chips are qualified for these grades (the AEC-Q100 standard for integrated circuits).

Supply: a nominal 12 V system runs between about 9 V and 16 V, sags while cranking, and sees fast spikes from switched coils and a load dump (the alternator suddenly losing its battery connection while charging).
Vibration, humidity, EMC: ECUs are sealed, and must neither disturb other systems nor be upset by ignition noise.
Safety and cost: brake and steering ECUs check themselves, and every part is made in millions.

blocks.text: All these parts are built from semiconductors, mostly silicon. A semiconductor conducts better than an insulator and worse than a metal. Pure silicon has an energy gap of 1.12 eV, so few electrons are free at room temperature. Doping adds a tiny amount of another element: phosphorus gives spare electrons (n-type), boron gives holes, missing electrons that act as positive carriers (p-type). Where p-type meets n-type a pn junction forms. It conducts in one direction once the forward voltage passes about 0.6 to 0.7 V and blocks in the other. Every diode, transistor and chip in this unit is built from such junctions. A junction's forward voltage falls by about 2 mV per kelvin as it warms.
An ECU board carries passive parts (resistors, capacitors, inductors), which only store or dissipate energy, and active semiconductor parts, which switch or amplify. The common ones and their jobs:

head: Component
What it does
Use in the vehicle
rows: Gives a coil's current a path at switch-off
Conducts in reverse above a set voltage
Clamps spikes on supply and sensor lines
Injector, lamp, motor and PWM drivers
MOSFET input, bipolar output, for high voltage
Microcontroller, regulator, CAN transceiver, smart switch

blocks.text: A bipolar transistor needs a base current IB; the collector current is about β times larger (β, the current gain, is often 50 to 300; a saturated switch is designed for a forced gain of only 10 to 20). Fully on, it drops 0.2 to 0.3 V (VCE(sat)). A MOSFET needs almost no steady gate current: a gate voltage of 5 to 10 V turns it on, and it then behaves like a small resistor RDS(on), often a few milliohms. Its loss is P = I² RDS(on). That is why output drivers are now MOSFETs, often packaged as smart power switches that add current limiting, over-temperature shut-down and a fault flag the microcontroller can read.

sections.h3: Microcontrollers and data processing in the vehicle

blocks.text: A microcontroller (MCU) is a processor with its memory and input-output on one chip. Engine ECUs use 32-bit MCUs clocked at tens to a few hundred megahertz. Its parts:

items: CPU: executes the program, one or more instructions per clock cycle.
Flash memory: holds the program and the calibration maps; keeps them with the power off.
RAM: working values that change every cycle (speed, load, counters); lost at power-off.
EEPROM or data flash: learnt values and stored fault codes that must survive switch-off.
ADC: turns sensor voltages into numbers (10 or 12 bits); timers with capture inputs time crank-tooth edges, and compare outputs and PWM channels fire injectors, coils and valves at exact moments.
Communication: CAN and LIN controllers to talk to other ECUs; watchdog: a timer that resets the MCU if the program stops refreshing it.

blocks.text: Data processing in the ECU follows one loop: read the inputs, check that each is plausible, compute, drive the outputs, and log faults. Fast events such as a crank tooth arrive as interrupts that pause the main loop. Slow ones (coolant temperature) are read every 10 to 100 ms. Most control laws are not equations but maps: tables over speed and load, read with linear interpolation. If a 2000 rpm cell holds 20° of spark advance and the 3000 rpm cell holds 26°, the ECU uses 20 + (26 − 20) × (2500 − 2000) ÷ (3000 − 2000) = 23° at 2500 rpm.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: One binary digit; 8 bits; the width the CPU handles at once (32 bits)
Cycles per second that pace the CPU, e.g. 80 MHz
A hardware signal that runs a short routine at once
Smallest step of a converter: V<sub>ref</sub> ÷ (2<sup>n</sup> − 1)
The result must come before a deadline (the next spark)

spec.aria: Block diagram. Crank, MAP and coolant sensors feed an input filter block, then a microcontroller containing ADC, capture timer, CPU at 80 megahertz, watchdog, flash, RAM and EEPROM. PWM outputs drive MOSFET drivers for an injector, an ignition coil and a 4.07 ampere lamp. A CAN and LIN block links other ECUs.

examples.question: An engine ECU has an 80 MHz microcontroller and a 60-2 crank wheel. (a) How much time and how many clock cycles pass between two tooth interrupts at 6000 rpm? (b) The tooth routine takes 1500 cycles. What share of the CPU does it use? (c) At what speed would the routine use half the CPU?
steps: Revolutions per second: 6000 ÷ 60 = 100 rev/s, so one revolution takes 10 ms.
Tooth pitch period: 10 ms ÷ 60 pitches = 0.1667 ms = 166.7 µs.
Clock cycles per tooth: 166.7 × 10⁻⁶ s × 80 × 10⁶ Hz = 13 333 cycles.
Load of the tooth routine: 1500 ÷ 13 333 = 0.1125, about 11 % of the CPU.
Half the CPU means 1500 cycles in a tooth period of 3000 cycles = 3000 ÷ 80 MHz = 37.5 µs. One revolution is then 60 × 37.5 µs = 2.25 ms, so n = 60 ÷ 0.00225 = 26 667 rpm.
Check: no road engine reaches 26 667 rpm, so the MCU has time left for injection, ignition and diagnosis.
examples.answer: 166.7 µs and 13 333 cycles per tooth; the routine takes about 11 % of the CPU at 6000 rpm and would reach 50 % only at about 26 700 rpm.

examples.question: A 55 W headlamp on a 13.5 V supply is switched (a) by a MOSFET with R<sub>DS(on)</sub> = 10 mΩ and (b) by a bipolar transistor with V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> = 0.3 V and a forced gain of 20 in saturation. Find the lamp current, the power lost in each switch, and the base current the bipolar transistor needs. Which can a microcontroller pin drive directly?
steps: Lamp current: I = P ÷ V = 55 ÷ 13.5 = 4.07 A.
MOSFET loss: P = I² R<sub>DS(on)</sub> = 4.07² × 0.010 = 0.166 W.
Bipolar loss: P = V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> × I = 0.3 × 4.07 = 1.22 W, more than seven times the MOSFET.

A microcontroller pin supplies only a few milliamps, so it cannot give 204 mA of base current. It can charge a logic-level MOSFET gate (nearly zero steady current), usually through a gate driver or inside a smart high-side switch.
examples.answer: I = 4.07 A; the MOSFET loses 0.166 W and the bipolar transistor 1.22 W and needs 0.204 A of base current. Only the MOSFET can be driven from the MCU (through a gate driver).

traps: A pn junction does not conduct at any forward voltage: silicon needs about 0.6 to 0.7 V first. Writing "a diode drops 0 V" loses the mark in rectifier questions.
MOSFET loss is I² R<sub>DS(on)</sub>, not V × I with the supply voltage; the supply voltage sits across the load, not the switch.
Flash and EEPROM both keep data at power-off: the program and maps live in flash, learnt values and fault codes in EEPROM.
A watchdog does not detect wrong sensor values; it detects a program that has stopped running and resets the MCU.

quiz.q: List four demands that the vehicle places on electronic control units.
quiz.a: Wide temperature range (−40 °C to 125 °C or more), a varying supply with spikes and load dump, vibration and humidity, electromagnetic compatibility; also long life, safety and low cost.

quiz.q: Why are n-type and p-type silicon made, and what does a pn junction do?
quiz.a: Doping gives free electrons (n-type, phosphorus) or holes (p-type, boron). Where the two meet, a junction forms that conducts in the forward direction above about 0.6 V and blocks reverse current: the basis of diodes and transistors.

quiz.q: Why have MOSFETs replaced bipolar transistors as ECU output drivers?
quiz.a: A MOSFET is voltage-controlled, so it needs almost no steady gate current, and its on-loss I²R<sub>DS(on)</sub> is small at milliohm resistance. A bipolar transistor needs a large base current and drops 0.2 to 0.3 V, wasting more power.

quiz.q: A spark map gives 18° at 40 kPa and 12° at 80 kPa (same speed). Find the advance at 55 kPa by linear interpolation.
An ECU resets now and then when the starter cranks on a cold morning. Analyse two causes and one design remedy.
quiz.a: The battery voltage sags under the starter load below what the regulator needs, so the MCU supply falls and the brown-out detector resets it; or the watchdog trips because the program stalls during the dip. Remedies: a low-drop regulator with a reservoir capacitor, or a supply that boosts during cranking; also check battery and earth resistance.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cars are moving from dozens of small ECUs to a few zone controllers with multicore MCUs, and silicon carbide (SiC) transistors are replacing silicon in electric-vehicle inverters. Search for AEC-Q100 grades, smart high-side switch, lockstep microcontroller and SiC MOSFET traction inverter.
